The Case for Sortition: Why Random Selection Could Save American Democracy

Introduction

American democracy stands at a crossroads. Public trust in government has plummeted to historic lows, congressional approval ratings hover in the teens, and the feeling that "the system is rigged" transcends partisan lines. Wealthy donors, career politicians, and entrenched party structures have created an ecosystem where ordinary citizens feel voiceless despite living in a nation ostensibly governed "by the people, for the people." Against this backdrop, an ancient idea deserves serious modern consideration: sortition, or the random selection of citizens to fill legislative and executive roles, much as jury duty functions today.

While this proposal is radical and would face enormous practical and constitutional obstacles, it raises questions that deserve thoughtful exploration. Below, I'll present the strongest arguments in its favor—while acknowledging that reasonable people can disagree about whether the cure might create its own problems.

1. Dismantling the Architecture of Political Corruption

The most persuasive argument for sortition is its potential to sever the link between wealth and political power. Today's electoral system creates a transactional relationship between candidates and donors. Running for Congress costs millions; running for president costs billions. This financial barrier doesn't just limit who can run—it shapes who does run and, critically, whose interests they serve once in office.

Research consistently shows that policy outcomes in the United States correlate more strongly with the preferences of economic elites and organized interest groups than with those of average citizens (Gilens & Page, 2014). Elections, rather than being a corrective to this imbalance, often reinforce it: candidates must court donors, lobbyists gain disproportionate access, and the revolving door between government and industry spins ever faster.

Sortition would make political corruption structurally almost impossible. You cannot bribe someone who doesn't know they will hold power. You cannot fund a campaign for a person who was selected by lottery. You cannot create a political machine when the "candidates" are drawn randomly from the entire population. The relationship between money and power—the beating heart of modern political corruption—would be severed at its root.

2. A Genuine Remedy for Hyper-Partisanship

America's two-party system has calcified into something the Founders explicitly warned against. George Washington's farewell address cautioned against "the baneful effects of the spirit of party," and yet partisanship has become the defining feature of modern governance. Elected officials increasingly vote along party lines regardless of the merits of legislation, demonize their opponents rather than debate policy, and treat compromise as betrayal.

Sortition would fundamentally alter this dynamic. Randomly selected citizens would not arrive in office owing loyalty to a party apparatus, having survived a partisan primary, or carrying a political brand they need to protect. They would bring their personal experiences, professional knowledge, and community perspectives—and little else. Without the need to appeal to a partisan base for re-election, these citizen-legislators would be freer to weigh evidence, listen to diverse viewpoints, and reach pragmatic conclusions.

This is not mere speculation. Historical and contemporary examples of deliberative bodies chosen by lot—such as the Athenian boule, various citizens' assemblies in Ireland, British Columbia, and elsewhere—have consistently demonstrated that diverse groups of ordinary people, when given good information and structured deliberation time, can reach thoughtful, nuanced, and broadly representative decisions. They often cut across ideological lines in ways that elected politicians cannot or will not.

3. True Representation: A Mirror of Society

The United States Congress is roughly 75% male, overwhelmingly white relative to the general population, and disproportionately composed of lawyers, business executives, and career politicians. The median net worth of a U.S. Senator exceeds $1 million; the median net worth of an American household is roughly $120,000. By almost every demographic measure, elected officials look nothing like the people they represent.

Sortition would instantly solve this representation gap. A randomly selected legislature would, by mathematical necessity, approximate the demographic composition of the nation—roughly proportional representation by race, gender, age, income, education, geography, and ideology. Working-class people, rural communities, young adults, and historically marginalized groups would gain representation not through the uncertain mechanism of electoral politics but as a matter of statistical certainty.

This matters not merely as a symbolic good but as a practical one. Policies are shaped by the lived experiences of those who craft them. A legislature that includes teachers, nurses, truck drivers, single parents, and small-business owners alongside the usual suspects would bring a breadth of practical knowledge that no amount of lobbying or testimony can replicate.

4. Empowering Ordinary Citizens

At its core, democracy rests on the idea that ordinary people are capable of self-governance. Yet the modern electoral system implicitly contradicts this premise by creating a professional political class—a group of people whose primary expertise is winning elections, not governing wisely. The skills that make someone a successful campaigner (charisma, fundraising ability, media savvy, willingness to make promises) are not the same as the skills that make someone a good policymaker.

Sortition takes the radical step of trusting citizens directly. It says: You are competent enough to serve. Your perspective matters. You don't need permission from a party, a donor network, or a political dynasty to participate in governing your country.

This empowerment extends beyond those who are selected. When people see someone like themselves—a neighbor, a coworker, a family member—serving in government, it rebuilds the sense of connection and ownership that democracy requires. Research on citizens' assemblies consistently shows that participants report transformative experiences: greater civic engagement, deeper understanding of policy complexity, and renewed faith in democratic institutions. These effects ripple outward to their communities.

5. Addressing the Competence Objection

The most common objection to sortition is that ordinary citizens lack the expertise to govern. This concern is understandable but overstated, for several reasons:

First, elected politicians are not policy experts either. Most are generalists who rely heavily on staff, advisors, and lobbyists for technical knowledge. A randomly selected citizen with a good support structure could perform similarly.

Second, sortition does not preclude expertise—it changes how expertise is accessed. Professional civil servants, policy analysts, legal counsel, and subject-matter experts would continue to exist. The role of the randomly selected representative would be to weigh competing values and make decisions, not to personally master every policy area. This is, in fact, what we already expect of elected officials.

Third, the diversity of knowledge in a randomly selected body is itself a form of expertise. A body that includes engineers, farmers, teachers, veterans, healthcare workers, and artists brings a collective intelligence that specialized politicians often lack. The 2008 financial crisis, for instance, was enabled in part by groupthink among people who shared similar backgrounds and assumptions.

6. Practical Considerations and Hybrid Models

Pure sortition—replacing every elected office with random selection—would raise legitimate concerns about accountability, continuity, and executive competence. A thoughtful implementation might therefore consider hybrid models:

  • A bicameral legislature where one chamber is elected and the other is selected by lot, combining democratic accountability with demographic representation.
  • Short terms of service (perhaps 2–3 years) with no possibility of re-selection, ensuring rotation and preventing the entrenchment of power.
  • Robust support systems including orientation programs, independent policy briefings, and administrative staff to help citizen-legislators navigate complex decisions.
  • Executive functions handled by appointed professionals (similar to how city managers operate in many municipalities), with randomly selected citizens providing oversight and direction.

Such hybrid models could preserve the benefits of sortition while mitigating its risks.

Conclusion

The American electoral system was a remarkable innovation in the 18th century, and elections will always play some role in democratic governance. But the system as currently practiced has drifted far from its ideals. It concentrates power among the wealthy, rewards tribalism over deliberation, and leaves millions of citizens feeling unrepresented and unheard.

Sortition offers a provocative alternative—one rooted in the oldest democratic traditions (both ancient Athens and Renaissance Florence used random selection extensively) and supported by modern research on deliberative democracy. It would dismantle the machinery of corruption, bridge partisan divides, create a truly representative government, and restore the radical democratic faith that ordinary people can and should govern themselves.

Is it a perfect solution? No. Is it worth serious, sustained consideration as a way to reimagine what American democracy could become? Absolutely. The question is not whether we can afford to experiment with sortition—it is whether we can afford to continue with a system that so many Americans have already lost faith in.

The real-world implementation of such a system would involve profound constitutional, legal, and cultural challenges that deserve equal scrutiny. Healthy democratic debate requires engaging seriously with radical ideas while maintaining clear-eyed awareness of their limitations.

The United States stands at a critical juncture. Our democratic system, once a beacon of hope, is increasingly perceived as a broken machine, corroded by the corrosive twin forces of political corruption and paralyzing partisanship. Elections, the cornerstone of our representative democracy, have demonstrably failed to deliver accountable, effective governance. It is time to confront this failure and embrace a radical, yet historically proven, alternative: replacing all elections for legislative and executive leadership with a system of sortition – the random selection of citizens to serve in government.

The most damning indictment of our current system is its inherent vulnerability to corruption. Elections are expensive, requiring vast sums of money to secure victory. This creates an inescapable dependency: candidates must court wealthy donors, corporations, and special interest groups. These entities, in exchange for financial support, demand favorable legislation, regulatory loopholes, and access to power. This is not merely a perception; it is a documented reality, evidenced by the revolving door between Congress and lobbying firms, the influence of Super PACs, and the consistent prioritization of donor interests over the public good. Sortition, by its very nature, eliminates this corrupting dynamic. Legislators and executives are chosen by lottery, not by purchase. They owe their position to chance, not to campaign contributors. Their sole obligation becomes serving the public interest, as they have no need to raise funds or repay debts. The random selection process inherently removes the financial incentive for corruption, fostering a legislature and executive branch composed of individuals whose primary motivation is civic duty, not personal enrichment or donor appeasement.

Furthermore, elections are the primary engine of political polarization and gridlock. The electoral process forces candidates into a zero-sum game, demanding they appeal to the extremes of their party base to secure the nomination. This necessitates demonizing opponents, embracing uncompromising ideological positions, and prioritizing partisan victory over pragmatic problem-solving. Once in office, representatives are bound by party loyalty, fearing primary challenges from the left or right more than they fear the electorate. This creates a legislative environment where compromise is seen as weakness, bipartisan cooperation is rare, and progress is stifled. Sortition, however, would dissolve these partisan incentives. Legislators selected by lottery would represent a true cross-section of the citizenry, not a narrow ideological faction. Their selection is random, not based on party affiliation or campaign promises. This diversity of background and perspective would naturally foster dialogue and compromise. When your fellow legislators are chosen alongside you by chance, the "us vs. them" mentality diminishes. The focus shifts from partisan warfare to finding solutions that benefit the community as a whole. A randomly selected body would be far more likely to engage in constructive debate, seek common ground, and enact legislation that reflects the complex, nuanced reality of the nation, rather than the rigid dictates of party orthodoxy.

Perhaps the most profound benefit of sortition is its power to empower ordinary people. In our current system, political participation is largely confined to voting every few years and occasional activism. The vast majority of citizens feel disconnected from the halls of power, viewing government as an elite institution inaccessible to them. Sortition shatters this illusion. It places the responsibility of governance directly into the hands of ordinary citizens. When a citizen's name is drawn from the pool, they are thrust into a position of immense responsibility and authority. This is not a symbolic gesture; it is a tangible transfer of power. Citizens suddenly become lawmakers, decision-makers, and stewards of the public trust. This experience is transformative. It forces individuals to engage deeply with complex issues, understand diverse perspectives, and develop the skills necessary for effective governance. It demonstrates that power is not the exclusive domain of career politicians or wealthy elites, but a responsibility that can be borne by any citizen willing to serve. This direct involvement fosters a profound sense of ownership and civic pride. Citizens who have served in government are far more likely to remain engaged, informed, and active in the political process long after their term ends. Sortition democratizes participation, moving beyond the passive act of voting to active, hands-on governance.

It is not about selecting the best people in an absolute sense, but about selecting a representative sample of the population. A randomly selected legislature would inherently possess the necessary diversity of skills, experiences, and perspectives found within the nation. Furthermore, the process can be designed to ensure a baseline of competence. For example, a pool could be drawn from citizens meeting certain basic qualifications (e.g., age, residency, literacy) and then stratified to ensure geographic, socioeconomic, and occupational diversity. Once selected, these citizens would have access to expert staff, comprehensive briefings, and the opportunity to learn on the job. The Athenian democracy, which employed sortition extensively for its most powerful bodies, produced remarkable statesmen and philosophers precisely because it harnessed the collective wisdom and judgment of a diverse citizenry. Competence is not the exclusive domain of career politicians; it emerges from diverse experience and a commitment to the public good.

Replacing elections with sortition is not a rejection of democracy; it is a refinement, a return to a more authentic form of popular sovereignty. It directly addresses the systemic failures of our current electoral system – the corruption fueled by money, the paralysis caused by hyper-partisanship, and the disempowerment of the citizenry. By randomly selecting citizens to serve in government, we create a legislature and executive that is truly representative, inherently less corrupt, and far more capable of transcending partisan divides. We empower ordinary people to take an active role in shaping their own destiny. The time has come to move beyond a system that serves the interests of the few and embrace a system that serves the people. Let us replace the broken machinery of elections with the powerful, equitable, and effective mechanism of sortition.

Introduction

Democracy in the United States is in crisis. Political corruption, partisan gridlock, and the overwhelming influence of money in elections have eroded public trust in government. By replacing elections with random selection, the United States could eliminate political corruption, reduce partisanship, and empower ordinary citizens—restoring faith in government and ensuring policies that truly reflect the public interest.

I. Sortition Eliminates Political Corruption

One of the most damaging aspects of the current electoral system is its susceptibility to corruption. Campaigns require massive funding, forcing candidates to rely on wealthy donors, corporate interests, and lobbyists. This creates a pay-to-play political culture where policies favor the rich and powerful rather than the average citizen.

A. The Corrupting Influence of Money in Elections

  • The 2020 U.S. elections cost $14.4 billion, more than double the 2016 spending (OpenSecrets).
  • Politicians spend 30-70% of their time fundraising instead of governing (Harvard Business Review).
  • Lobbyists and dark money shape legislation, leading to policies that benefit corporations over people—such as tax breaks for the wealthy, deregulation of polluting industries, and the revolving door between government and corporate jobs.

Sortition removes this corruption entirely. If leaders are selected by lot, they cannot be bought. There are no campaign contributions, no corporate sponsorships, and no quid pro quo politics. Instead, representatives would enter office with no financial obligations to special interests, ensuring that their decisions are made for the common good rather than personal or partisan gain.

B. No More Career Politicians

Elections create a professional political class that prioritizes reelection over governance. Incumbents manipulate district boundaries (gerrymandering), pander to extreme bases, and avoid controversial but necessary reforms to maintain power.

Sortition eliminates career politicians. Since representatives are chosen randomly for fixed terms (e.g., one year in a citizens' assembly), they have no incentive to game the system for personal advancement. Their only motivation is to serve the public interest during their brief tenure.

II. Sortition Reduces Partisanship and Polarization

America’s two-party system has devolved into hyper-partisanship, where compromise is seen as weakness and opposition is treated as an existential threat. This toxic polarization has led to government shutdowns, legislative gridlock, and even political violence.

A. Elections Incentivize Division

  • Primary elections push candidates toward extreme positions to appeal to base voters.
  • Gerrymandering creates safe seats where politicians only answer to their party’s fringe.
  • Media sensationalism rewards outrage over reasoned debate, deepening societal divisions.

Sortition removes these perverse incentives. Randomly selected citizens do not owe allegiance to a party—they represent themselves and their communities. Studies of citizens' assemblies (such as Ireland’s abortion and same-sex marriage referendums) show that when ordinary people deliberate without partisan pressure, they reach more moderate, pragmatic solutions.

B. Deliberation Over Demagoguery

Elections reward charisma over competence, leading to the rise of populist demagogues who exploit fear and division. Sortition, by contrast, selects everyday citizens who must engage in deliberative democracy—listening to experts, weighing evidence, and making decisions based on reason rather than rhetoric.

Research from the Deliberative Democracy Lab at Stanford found that randomly selected citizens, when given access to balanced information, make more informed and less polarized decisions than elected officials. This would shift politics from performance to problem-solving.

III. Sortition Empowers Ordinary Citizens

The greatest failure of the current system is its exclusion of ordinary people from meaningful political participation. Most Americans feel powerless, believing that government is run by and for an elite class. Sortition changes this by democratizing power.

A. True Representation, Not Elite Rule

  • Elections favor the wealthy and well-connected: Over 50% of Congress members are millionaires, while only 8% of Americans are (OpenSecrets).
  • Barriers to running for office (fundraising, name recognition, party backing) exclude working-class citizens.
  • Voter suppression and apathy mean that many voices—especially those of marginalized communities—are ignored.

Sortition ensures descriptive representation: the demographic makeup of the legislature would mirror the population in terms of race, gender, income, and education. This would lead to policies that address real-world concerns—such as healthcare, wages, and housing—rather than abstract ideological battles.

B. Restoring Trust in Government

Public trust in government is at near-historic lows, with only 20% of Americans trusting the federal government to do what is right (Pew Research). This distrust stems from the perception that politicians are self-serving and out of touch.

Sortition would restore faith in democracy by proving that government is by and for the people. When ordinary citizens—teachers, nurses, factory workers—are making decisions, the public would see that their voices matter. Experiments in participatory budgeting (where citizens directly allocate public funds) have shown that trust in government increases when people have a direct role in decision-making.

IV. Addressing Counterarguments

Critics of sortition raise several concerns, but none are insurmountable.

A. "Randomly Selected Citizens Aren’t Qualified!"

This objection assumes that elected officials are inherently more competent—yet Congress has an 11% approval rating (Gallup). Many politicians lack expertise in the issues they legislate, relying instead on staffers, lobbyists, and donors for guidance.

Sortition can be structured with educational safeguards:

  • Mandatory civic education before service.
  • Access to nonpartisan experts during deliberations.
  • Rotating terms to prevent entrenchment.

Studies show that ordinary citizens, when given proper information, make decisions as good as or better than elected officials (James Fishkin, Democracy When the People Are Thinking).

B. "Sortition Would Be Chaotic!"

Some fear that random selection would lead to inconsistent or irrational policies. However, sortition can be balanced with stability:

  • Hybrid models (e.g., a randomly selected legislative chamber alongside an elected one).
  • Supermajority requirements for major decisions to ensure broad consensus.
  • Professional civil service to provide continuity in administration.

Ancient Athens used sortition for centuries without collapse, and modern citizens' assemblies (like those in Ireland) have produced well-reasoned, widely supported policies.

C. "People Won’t Want to Serve!"

While some may resist civic duty, incentives and civic culture can ensure participation:

  • Stipends or salary replacements for those selected.
  • Civic lotteries as a norm, similar to jury duty.
  • Public recognition for service, fostering a culture of engagement.

In countries where sortition has been tested, most participants report the experience as deeply rewarding, increasing their political efficacy.

V. A Practical Path Forward

Transitioning to sortition would require gradual, strategic reforms:

  1. Pilot Programs: Start with local and state citizens' assemblies to demonstrate effectiveness (e.g., for budgeting, education policy, or climate action).
  2. Hybrid Systems: Replace one chamber of Congress (e.g., the Senate) with a sortition-based body while keeping the House elected.
  3. Constitutional Amendment: Eventually, amend the Constitution to phase out elections for legislative and executive branches in favor of stratified random selection (ensuring demographic representation).
  4. Public Education: Launch a national civic literacy campaign to prepare citizens for deliberative governance.

Conclusion

America’s electoral system is broken—corrupted by money, paralyzed by partisanship, and disconnected from the people. Sortition offers a radical but necessary solution: a government truly of, by, and for the people. By replacing elections with random selection, we can:

  • Eliminate political corruption by removing the influence of money.
  • Reduce partisanship by replacing career politicians with ordinary citizens.
  • Empower the public by ensuring that government reflects the diversity and interests of the nation.

Democracy should not be a privilege reserved for the wealthy and well-connected—it should be a shared responsibility. Sortition is not just a theoretical ideal; it is a practical, proven alternative that can restore faith in government and create a politics that works for everyone. The time has come to abolish elections and embrace democracy by lottery.

The Case for Sortition: Why Random Selection Is the Cure for American Democracy

For nearly two and a half centuries, Americans have worshipped at the altar of the ballot box, treating elections as the sacred cornerstone of self-governance. Yet as we survey the wreckage of our contemporary political landscape—billion-dollar campaigns, legislative paralysis, approval ratings for Congress that barely clear single digits, and a citizenry more polarized than at any point since the Civil War—we must confront an uncomfortable truth: elections have become the disease they were meant to cure. By replacing elections with random selection, the United States can eliminate the corruption inherent in campaign finance, dissolve the toxic partisanship that paralyzes governance, and finally realize the promise of true popular sovereignty by empowering ordinary citizens to govern themselves.

The most immediate and transformative benefit of sortition is the complete eradication of political corruption as we know it. Under our current electoral system, corruption is not an aberration but a structural inevitability. To win office, candidates must spend millions—sometimes billions—of dollars, creating an unavoidable dependency on wealthy donors, corporate PACs, and special interest groups. This financial arms race creates a tacit quid pro quo: the donor class funds campaigns, and elected officials deliver tax breaks, regulatory rollbacks, and subsidies in return. Even when no explicit bribes change hands, the "revolving door" between Capitol Hill and K Street ensures that politicians govern with one eye on their future lobbying careers rather than the public interest.

Sortition obliterates this entire ecosystem of influence. When representatives are chosen by lottery, there are no campaigns to fund, no advertisements to purchase, and no debates to sponsor. The randomly selected citizen who suddenly finds herself responsible for crafting education policy has made no promises to teachers' unions or charter school investors. She owes nothing to the pharmaceutical industry, the defense contractors, or the tech giants because she never asked for their money. Research from deliberative democracy experiments consistently shows that randomly selected citizens, freed from the need to fundraise for reelection, make decisions based on evidence and moral conviction rather than donor pressure. In Ireland’s 2016 Citizens’ Assembly, which used sortition to address constitutional questions including abortion rights, participants reported feeling liberated from party dogma and special interest pressure, resulting in recommendations that had stalled for decades under elected politicians.

Beyond eliminating corruption, sortition offers the only viable path to escaping the partisan death spiral that currently threatens to tear the nation apart. Elections, by their very nature, are zero-sum competitions that incentivize division. To mobilize voters, politicians must differentiate themselves from their opponents, often through fear-mongering and demonization. The primary system pushes candidates toward ideological extremes, while safe districts created by gerrymandering ensure that the only threat to an incumbent comes from the fringe, not the center. The result is a Congress where compromise is punished as betrayal and where the other party is treated not as loyal opposition but as existential enemy.

Random selection fundamentally alters these incentives. When a legislative body is chosen by lottery, it becomes a statistically representative sample of the American people—Democrats, Republicans, independents, and the politically disengaged sitting together as equals. The Case for Sortition: Why Random Citizen Selection Should Replace Elections in the United States

Introduction

The United States was founded on the principle that government derives its power from the consent of the governed. Yet today, that consent is often distorted by money, media manipulation, and the entrenched interests of political elites. Elections, while democratic in theory, have become a broken system—one that amplifies polarization, enables corruption, and disenfranchises ordinary citizens. The solution? Sortition—the selection of leaders by random citizen juries, a method used in ancient Athens and modern Iceland, could revolutionize American democracy by eliminating partisan politics, reducing corruption, and restoring power to the people.

This essay argues that replacing elections with sortition would:

  1. Eliminate political corruption by removing the influence of money and lobbyists.
  2. Reduce partisanship by selecting leaders based on merit rather than ideological loyalty.
  3. Empower ordinary citizens by giving them direct influence over governance.

If the U.S. is serious about reclaiming democracy from the oligarchy, sortition is not just a radical idea—it is the most practical path forward.

I. Elections Are a Failed System: Corruption, Polarization, and Disillusionment

The American electoral system is fundamentally flawed. While elections provide the illusion of choice, they are increasingly dominated by:

  • Corporate and wealthy interests – Campaigns are funded by billionaires, PACs, and dark money, ensuring that politicians prioritize donors over constituents.
  • Partisan extremism – Primary elections reward ideological purity over pragmatism, leading to gridlock and government shutdowns.
  • Voter suppression and apathy – Low turnout (especially among young and marginalized groups) means that elections are decided by the most engaged—but often the most extreme—voters.
  • Media manipulation – Social media algorithms and misinformation campaigns distort public perception, making elections a battleground for psychological warfare rather than policy debate.

The result? A political class that is less representative, more corrupt, and more disconnected from the people than ever before. If democracy is about the people ruling themselves, elections are failing spectacularly.

II. Sortition: A Proven Alternative to Elections

Sortition—selecting leaders by random lottery—is not a new idea. Ancient Athens used it to choose its governing councils, and modern experiments in Ireland, Canada, and the U.S. (such as citizen assemblies on climate change and healthcare) have shown that randomly selected citizens can make fair, informed, and pragmatic decisions.

How Sortition Would Work in the U.S.

  1. Random Selection – A pool of eligible citizens (registered voters) would be randomly chosen to serve in legislative bodies (e.g., Congress, state legislatures) or even executive roles (e.g., mayors, governors).
  2. Training & Compensation – Before taking office, selected citizens would receive paid training on policy, ethics, and governance to ensure competence.
  3. Term Limits & Rotation – Serving terms would be short (e.g., 1-2 years) to prevent entrenchment, with members rotating out to allow broad participation.
  4. Hybrid Systems Possible – Sortition could coexist with elections for some roles (e.g., judges, constitutional conventions) while replacing others entirely.

Why Sortition Works Better Than Elections

Problem with Elections Solution with Sortition
Money buys influence No campaign financing needed—leaders are chosen impartially.
Partisan extremism dominates Random selection reduces ideological bias; leaders must appeal to broad consensus.
Low voter turnout Every citizen has an equal chance to serve, increasing engagement.
Media manipulation distorts choices Decisions are based on evidence, not soundbites or ads.
Incumbency advantage No career politicians—leaders serve once and return to normal life.

III. Sortition Eliminates Political Corruption

One of the greatest failures of American democracy is its capture by corporate and financial elites. Politicians rely on donations, lobbyists, and corporate PACs to fund their campaigns, leading to:

  • Regulatory capture (e.g., Wall Street influencing financial laws).
  • Revolving door corruption (former officials becoming lobbyists).
  • Gerrymandering (districts drawn to favor incumbents and donors).

Sortition breaks this cycle because:

  1. No Campaign Financing Needed – If leaders are chosen by lottery, there is no need for fundraising, eliminating the influence of money.
  2. No Lobbyist Access – Randomly selected officials have no prior ties to corporate interests, making them less susceptible to bribes.
  3. Transparency & Accountability – Since no one can "buy" their way into office, corruption becomes nearly impossible.

Real-World Example: In Iceland’s 2010-2011 constitutional convention, a randomly selected citizen assembly drafted a new constitution—without corporate interference. The result was a more balanced, people-centered document than what politicians could have produced.

IV. Sortition Reduces Partisanship and Gridlock

American politics is defined by extreme polarization, where politicians prioritize party loyalty over governance. The two-party system forces leaders into ideological corners, leading to:

  • Government shutdowns (e.g., 2018-2019 budget battles).
  • Legislative gridlock (e.g., filibusters blocking bipartisan bills).
  • Populist backlash (e.g., Trump’s rise due to anti-establishment sentiment).

Sortition reduces partisanship because:

  1. No Primary Elections – Randomly selected leaders are not beholden to party bosses or ideological purists.
  2. Consensus Over Ideology – Without party labels, officials must negotiate and compromise, leading to more pragmatic policies.
  3. Broader Representation – Elections favor charismatic, extreme candidates; sortition ensures diverse perspectives without the need for partisan branding.

Evidence from Citizen Assemblies:

  • Ireland’s 2016 Abortion Referendum – A randomly selected jury recommended legalizing abortion, which voters later approved.
  • British Columbia’s 2004 Citizens’ Assembly on Electoral Reform – A random jury recommended proportional representation, leading to real electoral changes.
  • U.S. Climate Assemblies (e.g., Minnesota, Oregon) – Randomly selected citizens proposed carbon tax policies that politicians later adopted.

These examples show that ordinary people, given the right information, can make better decisions than career politicians.

V. Sortition Empowers Ordinary Citizens

The biggest flaw in American democracy is that power is concentrated in the hands of a permanent political class. Most citizens feel disconnected, ignored, or powerless—yet sortition would:

  1. Give Everyone a Chance to Lead – Unlike elections, where only a few can run, sortition ensures that any citizen could be selected, breaking the monopoly of elites.
  2. Increase Civic Engagement – If people know they might be called to serve, they are more likely to stay informed, debate issues, and participate in governance.
  3. Reduce Distrust in Government – When leaders are not career politicians, citizens may trust them more, reducing cynicism.

Psychological & Societal Benefits:

  • Reduces alienation – People see themselves as part of the system, not spectators.
  • Encourages civic education – If you might be selected, you’ll learn about policy, economics, and law.
  • Creates a more meritocratic system – Leadership is based on competence and fairness, not wealth or connections.

VI. Counterarguments & Rebuttals

Opponents of sortition raise several concerns, but none hold up under scrutiny:

1. "Random people aren’t qualified to govern!"

  • Rebuttal: Politicians are not inherently smarter than ordinary citizens. Many leaders (e.g., Abraham Lincoln, Ronald Reagan) were not career politicians before entering office.
  • Solution: Paid training and expert advisors ensure competence. (Example: Jury members in court are not lawyers, yet they make fair decisions with guidance.)

2. "Sortition would be too slow and inefficient!"

  • Rebuttal: Legislatures could be smaller and more focused (e.g., 500 randomly selected representatives instead of 435). Many decisions could be delegated to expert committees or digital democracy tools.
  • Example: Taiwan’s "VTaiwan" project uses online deliberation with randomly selected citizens to draft policies—faster than traditional legislatures.

3. "People would abuse the system!"

  • Rebuttal: Term limits and rotation prevent abuse. Unlike elected officials, who can build careers in politics, sortition leaders have no incentive to stay corrupt.
  • Example: In ancient Athens, randomly selected officials were held accountable by the people—if they failed, they could be prosecuted.

4. "It’s too radical—Americans won’t accept it!"

  • Rebuttal: Public support is growing. A 2021 YouGov poll found that 44% of Americans support using random citizen juries for policy decisions. Experiments in Ireland, Canada, and the UK show high approval rates.
  • Incremental Approach: Sortition could start with local governments, constitutional conventions, or advisory bodies before expanding.

VII. Conclusion: Sortition Is the Future of Democracy

The American electoral system is broken. It serves moneyed interests, fuels polarization, and leaves ordinary citizens feeling powerless. Sortition offers a radical but necessary alternative—one that: ✅ Eliminates corruption by removing money from politics. ✅ Reduces partisanship by selecting leaders based on merit, not ideology. ✅ Empowers citizens by giving everyone a chance to govern.

This is not about abandoning democracy—it’s about fixing it. Ancient Athens proved that ordinary people can govern wisely when given the chance. Modern experiments confirm it. The question is no longer whether sortition can work, but how soon we will implement it.

The time has come to replace elections with sortition—not as a perfect system, but as a fairer, more representative, and less corrupt way to govern. The people deserve no less.

Call to Action

If you believe in a democracy that works for all citizens, not just the wealthy and powerful, then:

  1. Support pilot programs (e.g., citizen assemblies on healthcare, climate, or elections).
  2. Advocate for constitutional amendments to allow sortition at the federal level.
  3. Demand transparency in how leaders are selected—why should we accept a system where billionaires decide our future?

The choice is clear: Keep the corrupt, partisan election system, or reclaim democracy through sortition. The future of governance depends on which path we choose.

Introduction

The current election system in the United States has significant flaws, including rampant political corruption, increasing partisanship, and the disenfranchisement of ordinary citizens. In this persuasive essay, I argue that replacing elections with a system of sortition – the selection of legislative and executive leaders through random citizen selection – can mitigate these issues and strengthen democracy.

Body

Political Corruption

One of the most pressing issues in American politics is political corruption. Elected officials often prioritize their own interests or those of their donors over the public good. A 2019 Gallup poll found that 53% of Americans believe corruption is widespread in the U.S. government (Saad, 2019). Sortition can prevent this by eliminating the incentives for corruption. Citizen legislators would serve short terms and would not have the financial resources or political connections that fuel corruption (Burnheim, 1985).

Reduced Partisanship

The U.S. political system has become increasingly partisan, leading to gridlock and inefficiency. Sortition could foster a more collaborative environment. Citizen legislators, selected at random, would not have pre-existing political affiliations or established networks, encouraging them to work together to find common ground (Gastil & Wright, 2019).

Empowering Ordinary People

Elections disproportionately favor the wealthy and the well-connected. Sortition, however, gives every citizen an equal chance of representing their community (Stone & Simpson, 2015). This inclusivity ensures that diverse perspectives are represented in government, leading to more informed decision-making and greater legitimacy.

Addressing Objections

Opponents of sortition might argue that random selection ignores existing expertise. However, citizen legislatures can still draw on external expertise through advisory committees or consultations with professionals (Mansbridge & Martin, 2013). Moreover, experience suggests that deliberative bodies can acquire enough knowledge to make informed decisions.

Another concern is that ordinary citizens might lack the skills or capacities for legislative work. However, studies show that training and support can effectively prepare inexperienced citizens for policymaking (Burnheim, 1985).

Conclusion

In conclusion, implementing a system of sortition in the United States can significantly ameliorate the issues of political corruption, partisanship, and the disenfranchisement of ordinary people. By giving every citizen an equal chance to participate in governance, sortition can broaden representation, promote collaboration, and enhance the legitimacy of our democracy. It is not a panacea for all political problems, but it offers a substantial step towards a more responsive and fair political system. Let us consider this ancient practice as a modern solution to reinvigorate American democracy.

Improved Government Fairness

Enhanced Democratic Representation
